title: Thomassen's Conjecture
statement_text: For all numbers $k$ and $g$ there exists $d=d(k,g)$ such that every graph of minimum degree at least $d$ contains a subgraph of minimum degree at least $k$ and girth at least $g$.
context_text: Thomassen's conjecture from 1983 is the central motivation of the paper. The authors initiate the systematic study of directed analogs, replacing minimum degree by minimum out-degree. An equivalent reformulation is that every graph containing a cycle is avoidable.
paper_contribution: Shows that the most direct extension of Thomassen's conjecture to digraphs (using minimum out-degree) is false; proves all orientations of $C_3$ and $C_5$ are avoidable; and fully characterizes which digraphs are avoidable when restricted to regular host digraphs.
paper_title: Extending Thomassen's conjecture to directed graphs

title: Conjecture 6.1
statement_text: All orientations of odd cycles are avoidable.
context_text: A digraph $F$ is avoidable if there is a function $d_F:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that every digraph of minimum out-degree at least $d_F(k)$ contains an $F$-free subdigraph (one with no copy of $F$) of minimum out-degree at least $k$. This is the directed analogue of Thomassen's conjecture, which in this language states that every undirected graph containing a cycle is avoidable (with minimum degree instead of out-degree); no forest is avoidable there. For undirected graphs all odd cycles are trivially avoidable, since every graph of minimum degree at least $2k-1$ has a bipartite subgraph of minimum degree at least $k$; for digraphs no such reduction exists, as Thomassen constructed digraphs of arbitrarily large minimum out-degree in which every directed cycle is odd. The authors prove that all orientations of $C_3$ and $C_5$ are avoidable (directed cycles of all lengths were known to be avoidable, by Dellamonica, Koubek, Martin and Rödl), while no one-directed complete bipartite graph (all arcs from one side to the other; this includes anti-directed even cycles) and no oriented forest is avoidable. A positive resolution would yield that every digraph of large minimum out-degree has a subdigraph of still large minimum out-degree whose underlying graph has large odd girth, a directed analogue of the existence of bipartite subgraphs of high minimum degree.
paper_title: Extending Thomassen's conjecture to directed graphs

title: Question 6.2
statement_text: Are all digraphs which allow a height function not avoidable?
context_text: A digraph $F$ is avoidable if there is a function $d_F:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that every digraph of minimum out-degree at least $d_F(k)$ contains an $F$-free subdigraph (one with no copy of $F$) of minimum out-degree at least $k$. This is the directed analogue of Thomassen's conjecture, which in this language states that every undirected graph containing a cycle is avoidable (with minimum degree instead of out-degree); no forest is avoidable there. A height function of a digraph $D$ is a map $h:V(D)\to\mathbb{Z}$ with $h(v)=h(u)+1$ for every arc $(u,v)$ (so a digraph allows one if and only if, in every cycle of the underlying graph, the numbers of forward and backward arcs are equal). The authors prove that all orientations of $C_3$ and $C_5$ are avoidable (directed cycles of all lengths were known to be avoidable, by Dellamonica, Koubek, Martin and Rödl), while no one-directed complete bipartite graph (all arcs from one side to the other; this includes anti-directed even cycles) and no oriented forest is avoidable. All digraphs shown not to be avoidable in the paper (one-directed complete bipartite graphs and oriented forests) allow a height function, which motivates asking whether allowing a height function characterizes, or at least implies, non-avoidability. The simplest digraph with a height function whose avoidability is unknown is the orientation of $C_4$ formed by two parallel directed paths of length two.
paper_title: Extending Thomassen's conjecture to directed graphs

title: Question 6.3
context_text: A digraph $F$ is avoidable if there is a function $d_F:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that every digraph of minimum out-degree at least $d_F(k)$ contains an $F$-free subdigraph (one with no copy of $F$) of minimum out-degree at least $k$. This is the directed analogue of Thomassen's conjecture, which in this language states that every undirected graph containing a cycle is avoidable (with minimum degree instead of out-degree); no forest is avoidable there. The undirected $C_4$ is avoidable (Thomassen's conjecture is known for $4$-cycles). The authors prove that no one-directed complete bipartite graph (all arcs going from one side to the other) is avoidable; in particular the anti-directed orientation of $C_4$ (alternating directions) is not avoidable, whereas the directed $C_4$ is avoidable (Dellamonica, Koubek, Martin and Rödl proved that all directed cycles are). A height function of a digraph $D$ is a map $h:V(D)\to\mathbb{Z}$ with $h(v)=h(u)+1$ for every arc $(u,v)$ (so a digraph allows one if and only if, in every cycle of the underlying graph, the numbers of forward and backward arcs are equal). The authors ask whether digraphs allowing a height function are never avoidable; the simplest digraph with a height function whose avoidability is unknown is the orientation of $C_4$ consisting of two parallel directed paths of length two. They believe this is the most difficult orientation of $C_4$ and that resolving the height-function question would likely also answer this one.
paper_title: Extending Thomassen's conjecture to directed graphs

title: Eulerian-avoidability characterization
context_text: A digraph is Eulerian if every vertex has the same in-degree as out-degree. A digraph $F$ is Eulerian-avoidable if there is $d_F:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that every Eulerian digraph with minimum out-degree at least $d_F(k)$ contains an $F$-free subdigraph (one with no copy of $F$) with minimum out-degree at least $k$; in the general (non-Eulerian) setting, $F$ is called avoidable. A digraph is $d$-regular if every vertex has in- and out-degree $d$, and $F$ is regular-avoidable if there is $d_F$ such that every $d_F(k)$-regular digraph contains an $F$-free subdigraph of minimum out-degree $k$; the authors prove that a digraph is regular-avoidable if and only if it is not a grounded forest (an oriented forest having a height function, i.e. $h(v)=h(u)+1$ for every arc $(u,v)$, that is constant on the vertices of in-degree at least $2$). In the general setting the characterization of avoidable digraphs is wide open (all orientations of $C_3$ and $C_5$ are avoidable, but no one-directed complete bipartite graph and no oriented forest is). Eulerian host digraphs are intermediate between the two settings, and the authors suggest that this question might yield a new approach to the undirected Thomassen conjecture (every graph containing a cycle is avoidable with respect to minimum degree). They propose as a starting point whether every orientation of $C_4$ is Eulerian-avoidable.
notes: Stated as a prose question immediately preceding the numbered Question 6.4; no labelled environment.

title: Question 6.4
context_text: A digraph is Eulerian if every vertex has the same in-degree as out-degree. A digraph $F$ is Eulerian-avoidable if there is $d_F:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that every Eulerian digraph with minimum out-degree at least $d_F(k)$ contains an $F$-free subdigraph with minimum out-degree at least $k$; without the Eulerian restriction on the host, $F$ is avoidable. In the general setting the authors show that the anti-directed $C_4$ (alternating directions) is not avoidable, the directed $C_4$ is avoidable (all directed cycles are, by Dellamonica, Koubek, Martin and Rödl), and the avoidability of the orientation formed by two parallel directed paths of length two is open. A digraph is $d$-regular if every vertex has in- and out-degree $d$, and $F$ is regular-avoidable if there is $d_F$ such that every $d_F(k)$-regular digraph contains an $F$-free subdigraph of minimum out-degree $k$; the authors prove that a digraph is regular-avoidable if and only if it is not a grounded forest (an oriented forest having a height function, i.e. $h(v)=h(u)+1$ for every arc $(u,v)$, that is constant on the vertices of in-degree at least $2$). The Eulerian setting sits between the two and might give new insight into Thomassen's undirected conjecture; this question is proposed as a starting point.
